PNANY Dashboard

Philippine Nurses Association of New York (PNANY) Leaders 2026–2028

Driven by Purpose,
United in Mission

Empowering Filipino Nurses in New York. PNANY is a non-profit nursing group, started in 1929. It speaks up for Filipino American nurses in New York State.

  • Laws and policy: fair treatment, safety, and respect for nurses in laws and regulations
  • Immigration and nurses trained abroad: help with licensing, jobs, and career advancement
  • Learning and growth: classes, leadership training, mentoring, and skill building for members and nonmembers
  • Community outreach: health education, wellness programs, and public service in Filipino American communities

Does PNANY support the UN Sustainable Development Goals?

In 2015 every UN member country agreed on 17 Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, each with specific targets[28]. A nursing association can't meet a country-level target on its own, but its work can push in the same direction[29]. This section maps PNANY's work to the targets it touches and rates how strong the public evidence is for each link.

PNANY's place among the 17 Goals

Pick a Goal to spotlight its targets. Brighter tiles have more links. The numbering follows the UN, but the official SDG icons and colors are not reproduced.

Evidence map: PNANY's work × UN targets

Each square is one link between an area of PNANY's work (rows) and a UN target (columns). Color shows how strong the public evidence is. Big squares are direct contributions; small squares support the target. Striped squares matter but have no public evidence yet. Click any square for details.

Click a square to see the evidence, the leaders involved and what would make the link stronger. A good place to start: the square where Continuing education meets target 3.c.

How strong is the evidence overall?

UN targets are written for countries, so PNANY contributes locally and partly. This mapping is the page author's reading of public information found on 13 November 2026 (PNANY's website, its "What's Happening" page and public event listings), offered as a starting point for discussion. If PNANY starts tracking numbers, such as nurses mentored, people screened or internationally educated nurses helped, these ratings could become measured results.

What happens when new members join?

Add up to three new members. Pick their skills, role and interests. Then run 5,000,000 practice runs of the next two years. In each run, links form month by month[14, 16]. How likely each link is comes from a model that learned from the current board[10, 11, 12]. People with shared skills, similar roles, a shared workplace or a shared mission area are more likely to link[15, 17]. Once a new member links with someone, they become more likely to link with that person's contacts too ("friends of friends")[7, 13]. The results show the most likely new links, how sure we can be, who connects different groups, and how the whole network changes.

Use this to explore "what if" questions. It cannot predict the future. The model learned from only 17 leaders and 18 public links, so its ranges are wide. Skills come from each leader's certificates and public job roles.

Statistical models: what the data can and cannot tell us

Nine ways of looking at the network. Each one answers one plain question. The results help with planning; they are not official predictions. PNANY's public data is small (17 leaders and 18 known leader-to-leader links), so many answers are "probably" or "too close to call," and the page says so.

Statistical models: path model, system dynamics, agent-based, regression, Bayesian, Monte Carlo, resilience, crisis surge, event footprint

What leads to strong links, and what do strong links lead to?

A path model draws our ideas as arrows[30, 31]. Each arrow is a hypothesis (H1 to H8). Boxes are things we can see in public data. Ovals are broader qualities measured through several signals, or not measured yet. Click any arrow to see its evidence.

Swipe sideways to see the whole model.

#HypothesisWhat the data says
For statisticians

H1–H4 are estimated with a Bayesian logistic dyad model (136 leader pairs, 18 ties; see the Bayesian tab) and checked with Firth-penalized logistic regression (Regression tab). H5 uses Spearman's rank correlation between layers active and betweenness (n = 17). H6–H8 need data PNANY has not published (membership, event attendance, retention), so they are shown as hypotheses from published research only. A full structural equation model[31] would need one row per member or event; with 17 leaders it would be badly underpowered, so the arrows are tested one at a time instead.

If we change one thing, where is membership in five years?

System dynamics treats the organization like connected tanks[33]. People flow from nurses who are not members yet to members to active volunteers. Word of mouth pulls more people in, the way new products spread[32]. Too much work on too few volunteers pushes people out.

Scenario:

Starting values are round numbers for easy reading (2,000 nurses not yet members, 120 members, 20 active volunteers, 17 leaders). They are not PNANY's real counts. The dashed lines show "no changes."

For modelers

Monthly steps, 60 months (Euler). join = (p + q·W·(M+A+L)/T) · N p = 0.001 outreach, q = 0.06 word of mouth × slider activate = 0.012 · M · (1 + mentoring) burnout = A · (0.02 + 0.06 · max(0, jobs/A − 1)) lapse = 0.012 · M dN = −join; dM = join − activate − lapse + burnout; dA = activate − burnout; L = 17 (held fixed) Loops: R1 word of mouth (more members → more joining); R2 mentoring (more mentoring → more volunteers); B1 volunteer strain (fewer volunteers → more burnout); B2 saturation (fewer nurses left to invite).

What happens when each nurse decides for themselves?

An agent-based model follows each person one at a time[34]. Each dot is a nurse at one of ten workplaces. Each week, a nurse may join if colleagues they know are members. Hearing it from two or more friends counts much more than one[9]. Members may start volunteering, and busy volunteers may step back.

  • Not a member yet
  • Member
  • Active volunteer
  • Leader
For modelers

280 nurses in 10 workplaces; about 5 contacts inside the workplace and 1 outside (a small world). 17 leaders and 25 members to start. Weekly, for each nurse: not a member → member: 0.0005 if no member contacts, 0.006 with one, 0.03 with two or more (×3 if a leader they know invites them) member → volunteer: 0.006 × (1 + volunteer and leader contacts) (×2 with mentoring) volunteer → member: 0.008 × (1 + max(0, 40 − volunteers) / 40) (strain when too few volunteers) member → lapsed: 0.002 Same random seed each reset, so runs can be compared.

Which shared traits go with two leaders being linked?

Logistic regression compares all 136 pairs of leaders: the 18 pairs publicly named together and the 118 pairs that are not[35]. An odds ratio above 1 means the trait goes with more links; below 1 means fewer. If the line crosses 1, we can't be sure.

Simulate it: how much would the answer change?

One fit of 136 pairs can be lucky or unlucky. The simulator refits the model hundreds of times. Resample draws new sets of 136 pairs from our own data, with repeats allowed[37]. Bigger network makes up pretend networks that follow the same pattern, to show how sure we would be with more leaders.

  • Our fit: best estimate

Who shows up in more layers?

A second, simpler regression (ordinary least squares) looks at the 17 leaders: how many layers each one is active in, compared with a graduate degree, a LinkedIn profile and a core-officer role.

TraitChange in layers95% range

For statisticians

Dyad model: Firth-penalized maximum likelihood (to handle few events and possible separation), Wald 95% intervals on the log-odds scale, 7 predictors. Dyads are not independent (each leader appears in 16 pairs), so the intervals are too narrow; treat p-values as rough. OLS: n = 17, 3 predictors, t-based 95% intervals (13 df). "On LinkedIn" is partly a measurement effect: LinkedIn is one of the main places links were found.

Leader pairs also share people, so they are not fully independent.

How sure can we be about each trait?

The Bayesian model gives each trait a range of likely values and the chance its effect is real (above zero)[36, 10]. The dot is the best estimate; the bar shows where it lands 90% of the time. The small hill shows all the likely values.

How are these values simulated?

  1. Start with a guess for how much each trait matters, close to zero (the "prior"). Four separate runs, or chains, start from different guesses.
  2. Try a small random change to the guess.
  3. Check it against the 136 leader pairs. If the new guess explains which pairs are linked better, keep it. If it explains them worse, sometimes keep it anyway, so the search can explore.
  4. Repeat thousands of times. The guesses that were kept pile up into the hills below. Where a hill sits, and how much of it is right of zero, is the answer[10, 36].

Each colored line is one chain. At first they wander from their starting guesses (the grey "warm-up" part, which is thrown away). When all four settle into the same band, they agree, and R-hat gets close to 1.00.

For statisticians

logit P(tieij) = β0 + Σ βkxijk; priors β0 ~ N(−1.5, 2²), βk ~ N(0, 1.5²). Adaptive random-walk Metropolis, 4 chains × 60,000 iterations, 15,000 burn-in, thinned to 2,000 draws; split R-hat shown below. AUC is in-sample. Categories: almost certainly (P > 95%), probably (P ≥ 80%), too close to call (otherwise), with the same thresholds for a negative effect.

Across millions of possible futures, what usually happens?

Monte Carlo means running the same uncertain story many times with different random draws, then counting the results[10, 16]. The New members simulator does this 5,000,000 times. Each run draws a new set of link strengths from the Bayesian model above, so the results carry its uncertainty forward.

  • Input: up to three new members with their skills, roles and interests.
  • Each run: two years, month by month; links form by chance, more often between similar people and through friends of friends[13, 15].
  • Output: the most likely new links, how sure we can be, who connects groups, and how the whole network changes.

What if a leader steps away?

Click any leader on the map to take them out, and watch what stays connected. Leaders who get cut off from the main group turn red. This is a stress test: networks that lean on a few people can break apart when those people leave[42, 43].

By default the roster layer is left out, because being listed on the same board connects everyone to everyone and hides real weak spots. Turn on "Count the roster as a link" to see the difference.

How fast does it fall apart?

The chart removes leaders one at a time: in a random order (500 tries, averaged) or the best-connected first. The chart shows what share of all 17 leaders stay in the main connected group. The lower line shows how much faster the network breaks when its key people leave.

Graph: all 32 nodes (17 leaders, PNANY, 10 organizations, 4 mission areas) with links from the workplace, co-mention, earlier-service and mission layers (and the roster layer when switched on). "Still connected" = number of the 17 leaders in the largest connected piece. Targeted removal goes by degree, recomputed after each removal. Random removal averages 500 random orders.

When a crisis hits, can PNANY keep up?

Pick a crisis and set how bad it is. The model plays out 26 weeks: how fast word reaches volunteers through the network, how many can help, how tired they get, and how much need goes unmet. It follows standard system dynamics methods[33], a word-of-mouth spread curve[32], a burnout loop like Homer's worker burnout model[44], and research on volunteers in emergencies[45]. The alert speed comes from the real network: a message passed from leader to leader through shared workplaces, co-mentions and mission teams reaches … leaders in … steps. The rest are reachable only through the board roster.

Crisis:

Need is shown as requests for help per week (for example, nurses needing license guidance, shifts to cover, or health-fair volunteers). Numbers are scenario-based, not PNANY records.

For modelers

Weekly steps, 26 weeks. need(t) = base + severity · peak · shape(t) (shape: fast spike, slow wave, or long plateau by crisis type) informed(t) = logistic spread; speed = 1 / (network steps to reach all leaders) × (2 with phone tree) capacity(t) = volunteers · informed · (1 − fatigue) · 3 requests each + partners · 25 fatigue(t+1) = fatigue + 0.08 · max(0, need/capacity − 1) − recovery (0.04, or 0.08 with backup pairs) unmet(t) = max(0, need − capacity)

What is the carbon footprint of a PNANY event?

Plan an event and compare holding it in person, hybrid and fully online. Travel usually matters most, then food. Online meetings use a little electricity for laptops and the internet[41]. Factors come from the U.S. EPA[38, 39] and published meal estimates[40]. The method follows the Greenhouse Gas Protocol for travel and purchased goods[46]. This supports UN Goal 13, Climate Action[28].

Start from:

For modelers

kg CO2e per passenger-mile (EPA 2025): car 0.2986 per vehicle-mile ÷ people per car; subway/bus 0.094; commuter rail 0.134; short-haul flight 0.209 (400 miles round trip). NYC grid (eGRID2023, NYCW): 976.1 lb CO2e/MWh = 0.443 kg/kWh. Venue: 0.5 kWh per person-hour (assumption). Meals (kg CO2e each): standard 2.585, less meat 1.103, vegetarian 0.51; snacks 0.3 (assumption). Online: 30 W laptop + 1.2 Mbps video at 0.06 kWh/GB ≈ 0.062 kWh per person-hour. Hybrid: online share stays home; the rest travel. Fully online: everyone online, no venue or catering.

What the numbers show

All 17 leaders, ranked
PersonRoleLinksLayers activeSpread across layersGo-between scoreGroupLinkedIn

Spread across layers[1] runs from 0 to 1. Near 1 means a person has links in many layers. Near 0 means their links are in only one layer. Go-between score[3] shows how often a person sits on the shortest path between two other people, so a high score means they connect others. Groups were found with a standard method that looks for people who are more linked to each other than to everyone else. Every link comes from public information found on 13 November 2026. Eight members had no public profile we could confirm, so their low scores mean missing information, not low importance. No photos were collected.

What the network sounds like

Hear the network played by a small orchestra[20, 21], then compare it with a healthy reference network: the same 17 leaders, imagined as a cohesive, strong, lively, nurturing and growing organization, played with exactly the same rules. Each layer of the network is one section of the orchestra. When leaders are well connected, their notes land in tune and blend into rich chords[23, 24]. Where connections are missing, notes drift off pitch and clash, so you can hear where the network needs work. The background music and sound effects pause while the piece plays and come back when it ends or you press Stop.

This is the score of the whole piece. Time runs left to right, and each row is one section of the orchestra. Each dot is a note. Colored dots are in tune; red dots with a wavy mark are out of tune. During playback a white line moves across, and the harmony meter shows how in tune the music sounds at that moment.

How to listen

Each layer is a section of the orchestra. Roster = cellos, Workplaces = French horns, Co-mentions = violins, Earlier PNANY service = clarinets, Mission work = harp.

In tune = well connected. A leader with public links in three or more layers plays perfectly in tune[1]. Fewer links and the notes drift off pitch.

A clash = a missing connection. A sour, wavering note marks a leader with no public link beyond the roster. It means missing public information, not low importance.

Two notes in a row = a link with a direction. Two notes at once = a two-way link, heard in the violins.

A held string chord underneath = cohesion. The more leaders are mentioned together, the fuller and steadier it sounds[9].

The closing chord = strength. Each section plays as loudly and as in tune as the share of leaders it reaches.

A rising harp run = a bridge. One leader active in several layers[8]. More notes mean more layers.

A bright celesta sparkle = a new member joins. Heard in the reference, followed by that member's first links.

Left and right = position on the map. Links on the left of the network map play in your left ear.

What the network sounds like right now
PNANY now vs. a healthy network

The healthy reference is an illustration, not a real network or a forecast. It keeps the real roster and adds the links a thriving organization would have: everyone mentioned together with several colleagues, every leader active in mission work (including immigration), most leaders with earlier PNANY service, and six new members joining over time.

Every orchestra has an open chair

Did you hear the notes that drift and clash? They aren't mistakes. Each one marks a link that isn't there yet, a seat no one has filled. Pick what you could bring, then hear how the music changes.

Research backs the idea: new links between groups open up ideas and help[7, 8], people take part more when several people they know take part[9], professional nursing groups give members networking, learning and a shared voice[25], and support from colleagues helps nurses trained abroad settle in[26, 27].

What is supported by research, and what is not
  • Supported: the network measures (layers, links, go-between score, groups, spread across layers) are standard methods [1–6]. Friend-of-friend linking, bridges between groups and the pull of close-knit groups are well studied [7–9]. The simulator follows standard ideas about how networks grow: people link with similar others, through shared groups and through friends of friends, one step at a time [10–17]. Joining a professional nursing group brings networking, learning and a shared voice [25], and support from colleagues helps nurses trained abroad settle into practice [26, 27].
  • Supported: people generally hear some note combinations as pleasant and stable and others as rough or clashing [23, 24], and data can be turned into sound in a repeatable way [20–22].
  • Simulations: every model and simulation on this page uses accepted methods from the research above, but the inputs are public information plus stated assumptions. Each one carries an "About these results" note that explains its limits.
  • Not yet tested: the simulator's numbers are forecasts from a small model (17 leaders, 18 known links), not observed results. The harmony score, the open chair seat model and the healthy reference network were designed for this page. They build on the research above, but no study has checked that they measure how healthy an organization is. Treat them as a way to start a conversation, not as a test result.
  • Limited by public data: every link comes from public, professional sources. A leader with few public links may still be very active; the page can only show what is posted online.
